title: His mother stood (John 19:25–27)
hook: Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple as his mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember me: a dying thief asked for one thing and was promised a garden. Your line was this day in paradise. Now, the ones who stayed.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Nothing to do. Nothing to fix. People stay because leaving is unthinkable. Now, the hill. Mark says that at the arrest his disciples all left him and fled. But John's Gospel slows down and names who is standing by the cross: his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen. And one disciple, never named, whom the Gospel calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. They can't stop it. They can't change any of it. They stand.
screen: `NOTHING TO FIX. THEY STAY.` → `THE WOMEN AND ONE DISCIPLE.` → `THEY STAND.`

segments.voice: Jesus spends some of his last words on this. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, behold thy son." And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." John adds: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman can sound cold in English. In John it's the same word he used for her at the wedding at Cana, a word of respect, and some readers hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis. Catholics hear this moment two ways, and hold both. The first is simple and human: a dying son makes sure his mother will have a home. The second is bigger. The Gospel never names the beloved disciple. Tradition says it was John. Some readers say leaving him unnamed lets every disciple stand in his place. So Catholics read it as Jesus giving his mother to all of us, and they call Mary the Mother of the Church, a title Pope Paul VI gave her during the Second Vatican Council. Then there's the word stood. In the Latin Bible the verse opens with stabant, they stood, all of them together. A medieval hymn takes the word for her alone: Stabat Mater, the mother stood. It belongs to the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows, and parishes sing it at the Stations of the Cross. She didn't faint. She didn't leave. She stood.
screen: `WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.` · `A SON MAKES SURE HIS MOTHER HAS A HOME.` · `THE DISCIPLE IS NEVER NAMED.` · `STABAT MATER: THE MOTHER STOOD.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who mothered you, by birth or not: a mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, and see their face. Then bring to mind someone who may have no one looking after them, an older woman on your street, a mother raising children alone, and choose one practical thing for them: a meal, a ride, an hour. If you pray, you can ask Mary to look after them too.
Stabat Mater. Latin for the mother stood, a hymn for Mary keeping watch at the foot of the cross.
Your line: behold thy mother. From that hour, she had a home. Day sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: Catholics sing or pray the Stabat Mater during the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, and honor Mary as Mother of the Church on the Monday after Pentecost.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 19:26–27 given from memory; confirm.
John 19:25: whether 'his mother's sister' and 'Mary of Cleophas' are one or two women is debated; the script lists them as the Douay-Rheims order reads, allowing either.
'Woman' as a term of respect and the Cana echo (John 2:4); the Genesis echo is a patristic and modern reading. Confirm.
Paul VI proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church on 21 November 1964, at the close of the third session of Vatican II; memorial on the Monday after Pentecost since 2018. Confirm.

Stabat Mater: 13th-century, often attributed to Jacopone da Todi; used as the sequence for Our Lady of Sorrows and commonly sung at the Stations. 'Sung on Good Friday' is customary rather than prescribed; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: the teach said the Latin Bible's word is stabat; the Vulgate of John 19:25 reads stabant (they stood), and the hymn takes stabat for Mary alone. Fixed. Also: hook no longer opens 'Think about' or tells the listener what they sat through; 'four women' (a count John does not settle) became 'the women', and the names follow the Douay-Rheims ('Mary of Cleophas', not 'the wife of'); cut 'who can barely breathe', 'can't get close enough to wipe his face' (contradicts 'stood by the cross') and 'widowed' (not in the text); 'most had fled' now attributed to Mark 14:50; 'every disciple stands in his place' attributed to some readers; 'sung on Good Friday' replaced by the Our Lady of Sorrows feast and the Stations; the practice no longer repeats day 61's 'stay with one person's pain' and now follows the line (take someone in).
